(CNN) -- Italian newspapers, an archbishop and civil liberties campaigners expressed shock and revulsion on Monday after photographs were published of sunbathers apparently enjoying a day at the beach just meters from where the bodies of two drowned Roma girls were laid out on the sand. Photographs of the dead Roma girls on a beach caused outrage in Italy. Italian news agency ANSA reported that the incident had occurred on Saturday at the beach of Torregaveta, west of Naples, southern Italy, where the two girls had earlier been swimming in the sea with two other Roma girls. Reports said they had gone to the beach to beg and sell trinkets. Local news reports said the four girls found themselves in trouble amid fierce waves and strong currents. Emergency services responded 10 minutes after a distress call was made from the beach and two lifeguards attended the girls upon hearing their screams. Two of them were pulled to safety but rescuers failed to reach the other two in time to save them.  Watch why the photos have generated anger » . The Web site of the Archbishop of Naples said the girls were cousins named Violetta and Cristina, aged 12 and 13. Their bodies were eventually laid out on the sand under beach towels to await collection by police. Photographs show sunbathers in bikinis and swimming trunks sitting close to where the girls' feet can be seen poking out from under the towels concealing their bodies. A photographer who took photos at the scene told CNN the mood among sunbathers had been one of indifference. Other photos show police officers lifting the bodies into coffins and carrying them away past bathers reclined on sun loungers. "While the lifeless bodies of the girls were still on the sand, there were those who carried on sunbathing or having lunch just a few meters away," Italian newspaper La Repubblica reported. Corriere della Sera said that a crowd of curious onlookers that had formed around the bodies quickly dispersed. "Few left the beach or abandoned their sunbathing. When the police from the mortuary arrived an hour later with coffins, the two girls were carried away between bathers stretched out in the sun." The incident also attracted condemnation from the Archbishop of Naples, Cardinal Crecenzio Seppe. "Indifference is not an emotion for human beings," Seppe wrote in his parish blog. "To turn the other way or to mind your own business can sometimes be more devastating than the events that occur." Recent weeks have seen heightened tensions between Italian authorities and the country's Roma minority amid a crackdown by Silvo Berlusconi's government targeting illegal immigrants and talk by government officials of a "Roma emergency" that has seen the 150,000-strong migrant group blamed for rising street crime. That has provided justification for police raids on Roma camps and controversial government plans to fingerprint all Roma -- an act condemned by the European Parliament and United Nations officials as a clear act of racial discrimination. Popular resentment against Romanies has also seen Roma camps near Naples attacked and set on fire with petrol bombs by local residents. In a statement published on its Web site, the Italian civil liberties group EveryOne said Saturday's drowning had occurred in an atmosphere of "racism and horror" and cast doubt on the reported version of events, suggesting that it appeared unusual for the four girls to wade into the sea, apparently casting modesty aside and despite being unable to swim. "The most shocking aspect of all this is the attitude of the people on the beach," the statement said. "No one appears the slightest upset at the sight and presence of the children's dead bodies on the beach: they carry on swimming, sunbathing, sipping soft drinks and chatting." CNN's Jennifer Eccleston contributed to this report.

**TORREGAVETA, Italy (CNN)** — Under the blazing midday sun on a crowded beach near Naples, holidaymakers laughed, sunbathed, and ate lunch. But just yards away, lying on the sand and covered by makeshift beach towels, were the lifeless bodies of two young girls.

The drowning of two Roma sisters at Torregaveta beach in July 2008—and the apparent indifference of the crowd around them—has ignited a wave of shock and self-examination across Italy, highlighting deep-seated racial tensions and raising painful questions about human empathy.

According to local authorities, 12-year-old Cristina Dobre and her 11-year-old sister, Violetta, had traveled to the beach from a nearby makeshift Roma camp. Like many impoverished children in the region, they were selling trinkets to tourists before deciding to wade into the sea to cool off.

Witnesses said a sudden change in sea currents swept the young girls away. Despite brief efforts by rescuers to save them, the sisters were pulled from the water unconscious and pronounced dead at the scene.

What followed, however, shocked the nation even more than the tragedy itself. 

Photographs published by Italian newspapers captured a stark, disturbing scene: as the small, towel-draped corpses lay awaiting the arrival of a coroner's hearse, beachgoers continued their summer routines. Sunbathers lounged on deck chairs, families unpacked picnic lunches, and couples strolled along the shore—scarcely looking at the drowned children just steps away.

The images quickly circulated around the globe, prompting international outrage and intense domestic debate.

### 'A Black Mark on Humanity'

Religious leaders, politicians, and human rights advocates expressed horror at the reaction of the crowd.

"To see the bodies of two children lying on the shore while people carry on as if nothing happened is a black mark on our humanity," said Cardinal Crescenzio Sepe, the Archbishop of Naples, in a passionate response to the incident. "This is not the Naples I know, nor is it the Italy we should accept."

Human rights groups argued that the indifference was emblematic of a broader, systemic bias against the country's Roma minority, often disparagingly referred to as "gypsies."

"If those had been two middle-class Italian children, the beach would have cleared, the atmosphere would have been one of collective grief," said Laura Boldrini, then a spokesperson for the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) in Italy. "The photos show a terrifying detachment from the suffering of others simply because of who they were."

### A Climate of Tension

The incident occurred during a period of heightened hostility toward the Roma community in Italy. Earlier that year, the government under Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi had declared a national state of emergency regarding Roma camps, implementing controversial measures that included fingerprinting camp residents, including children.

Media reports at the time frequently linked Roma communities to petty crime, fueling public fear and prejudice. Months prior to the drowning, a Roma camp near Naples was burned down by local residents in a vigilante attack following unverified rumors of an attempted kidnapping.

Critical observers argued that months of anti-Roma political rhetoric had effectively dehumanized the minority group in the eyes of the general public.

### A Community Defends Itself

As the outcry grew, some locals and witnesses pushed back against the narrative of cold indifference, arguing that the photographs painted an unfair picture of the scene.

Coast Guard officials noted that several beachgoers had initially rushed into the water to try to rescue the girls when the alarm was raised. Others claimed that the sunbathers remained on the beach simply because there was nowhere else to go while waiting hours for emergency services to clear the scene.

"People were stunned, they didn't know what to do," one local resident told Italian reporters at the time. "It wasn't malice; it was paralysis."

Yet for many, the imagery of casual beach life proceeding beside the bodies of dead children remains a haunting symbol of societal fracture.

The bodies of Cristina and Violetta were later returned to their family for burial in their home country of Romania. But the ghost of that summer day at Torregaveta continues to serve as a grim reminder of how thin the boundary can be between everyday life and profound moral failure.

The photograph, published across major Italian dailies, shows two holidaymakers casually sunbathing and eating lunch on the sand at Torregaveta, near Naples. Just a few feet away lie the sheet-covered bodies of two young Roma sisters, aged 11 and 12, who had drowned moments earlier.

The tragedy occurred on July 19, when Cristina and Violetta Dobreva, who lived in an informal encampment on the outskirts of Naples, entered the water to cool off after a morning spent selling trinkets along the coast. Caught in strong currents, the girls quickly sank beneath the waves. Despite the efforts of lifeguards, who pulled them from the water, resuscitation attempts failed. 

Their bodies were laid out on the sand, covered with beach towels and white sheets, to await the arrival of the coroner. Yet, according to witnesses and local reporters, the surrounding crowd of beachgoers barely paused their activities. Within an hour, life on the crowded beach returned to normal; families continued swimming, playing beach volleyball, and enjoying picnics in full view of the corpses.

### A "Picture of Shame"

The image of the sunbathers turning their backs on the dead girls sparked an immediate outcry across Italy’s political and social spectrum, sparking accusations that the nation has lost its moral compass.

Italy’s prominent daily *La Repubblica* published the image on its front page under the headline "The Picture of Shame," lamenting the total collapse of human empathy. 

"When the sea throws up two dead children, and the response of the beach is to keep sunbathing as if nothing happened, it means we have reached a point of no return," wrote commentator Laura Laurenzi in *La Repubblica*. "It is as if those girls were not human beings, but trash to be ignored until the municipal authorities come to clear it away."

*Corriere della Sera*, the nation’s leading newspaper, echoed the sentiment, describing the scene as a "chilling portrait of indifference." In a bitter column, the paper asked: "What has happened to our humanity? How can a mother watch her own children play in the sand while two deceased children lie abandoned next to her?"

### Church and Human Rights Leaders React

Religious figures were among the most outspoken in condemning the behavior of the bystanders. 

Cardinal Crescenzio Sepe, the Archbishop of Naples, issued a scathing statement condemning the lack of solidarity and common humanity displayed on the beach.

"To turn your back on two dead children, to continue sunbathing as if nothing has happened, is a gesture that hurts the heart," Cardinal Sepe said. "This is not Naples. This is not human. It is a sign of a society that is losing its soul, where the culture of indifference has suffocated the most basic human instincts."

Human rights and civil liberties groups quickly pointed out that the public’s indifference was inextricably linked to the identity of the victims. Roma communities in Italy face pervasive discrimination, and activists argued that the sunbathers' reaction was a direct result of the dehumanization of Roma people.

Roberto Malini, co-president of the civil rights group EveryOne Group, called the incident a "tragic symptom of a deeply racist climate."

"The photograph is a symbol of the moral degradation of a society that no longer recognizes the humanity of Roma people," Malini said in a statement. "If those two girls had been white, Italian children, the entire beach would have been in mourning. The sea would have been cleared, and people would have knelt in prayer. Instead, because they were 'gypsies,' their deaths were treated as a minor inconvenience to a summer weekend."

Amnesty International Italy also issued a stern warning, noting that "when a society normalizes the idea that certain human lives are worth less than others, total moral apathy is the inevitable result."

### The Shadow of Berlusconi’s Anti-Roma Policies

The tragedy occurred amidst a political climate increasingly hostile toward marginalized communities, specifically under the right-wing coalition government led by Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi. 

Since taking office earlier in the year, Berlusconi’s government—strongly influenced by its anti-immigrant coalition partner, the Northern League (*Lega Nord*)—had adopted an aggressive stance against the country's estimated 160,000 Roma residents. 

Interior Minister Roberto Maroni had declared the presence of Roma camps a "national security emergency." Among the government’s most controversial measures was a plan to register and fingerprint all inhabitants of Roma camps across Italy, including young children—a policy that drew fierce condemnation from the European Union, the United Nations, and the Vatican, who drew parallels to Europe's dark past.

Critics argue that state-sanctioned rhetoric framing Roma people as criminals, threats, and "unadaptable" elements of society created a social permission structure for the coldness displayed on the Torregaveta beach.

"The government has spent months telling the Italian public that Roma people are a danger, a plague, and an eyesore," said an activist from the anti-racism group *Arcigay*. "When the state treats a minority group like subhumans, you cannot be surprised when ordinary citizens step over their dead bodies on a beach."

While government ministers expressed grief over the loss of the two young lives, they largely rejected claims that state policies were to blame for the crowd's reaction, chalking the incident up to individual callousness. 

However, for many Italians, the haunting photograph remains an indelible stain. As the bodies of Cristina and Violetta were finally taken away in a black hearse late that afternoon, the sunbathers at Torregaveta remained on their towels—a stark, troubling portrait of modern indifference.

The funeral for Violetta and Cristina was attended by local officials, community members, and religious leaders attempting to offer the dignity in death that was denied to them in their final moments on the sand.

Years later, the Torregaveta drowning remains one of the most infamous examples of modern public indifference. The photograph of the scene is frequently referenced in ethical studies, sociology, and journalism as a tragic case study of human empathy failing in real time.

**NAPLES, Italy (CNN)** — The midsummer heat at Torregaveta beach, just west of Naples, was typical for a July afternoon in southern Italy. Families laid out bright towels, children splashed in the surf, and sunbathers soaked up the Mediterranean sun. 

Then came the tragedy. And shortly after, a chilling display of apathy that has sparked international outrage and forced Italy to confront a growing crisis of racial hostility.

Cristina Dobre, 11, and her 12-year-old sister, Violetta, had traveled to the beach from a nearby makeshift Roma camp to sell trinkets. Looking to escape the oppressive heat, the young girls entered the water. Neither could swim. Caught in a sudden, powerful current, they quickly drifted out of reach, screaming for help. 

By the time coast guard officials pulled them from the water, it was too late. Resuscitation attempts failed, and the girls were pronounced dead at the scene.

What happened next, however, has drawn severe condemnation across Europe. 

After coast guards wrapped the young sisters' bodies in white sheets and laid them side-by-side on the sand to await the arrival of the coroner, the beach routine resumed almost instantly. Just feet away from the lifeless corpses, tourists continued to sunbathe, read books, and eat picnic lunches. Photographs published worldwide showed a couple relaxing under an umbrella, completely unperturbed by the two small, sheet-covered bodies lying in the foreground.

The images have provoked horror across the globe and fueled an intense debate within Italy over moral bankruptcy and systemic racism against the Roma minority.

Italian media responded with swift and devastating criticism. Rome's daily newspaper *La Repubblica* splashed the photographs across its front page under a damning headline: "The Beach of Indifference." 

"While two little girls lay dead on the sand, people kept swimming, eating, and taking the sun," wrote *La Repubblica* columnist Sebastiano Messina. "It was as if the dead girls belonged to another species, as if their deaths were merely a temporary inconvenience to a summer vacation."

Another major national outlet, *Corriere della Sera*, described the scene as a "stain on the conscience of the nation," questioning how a society renowned for its family values could turn its back on dead children simply because of their ethnic background.

The religious community added its voice to the chorus of condemnation, led by the Archbishop of Naples, Cardinal Crescenzio Sepe. In an unusually direct and passionate statement, the Cardinal expressed his deep sorrow and shame over the incident.

"To pass by two lifeless bodies of children on a beach and carry on as if nothing happened—as if it were a matter of no concern—is a tragedy far greater than the drowning itself," Cardinal Sepe said. "This is not just a tragedy of nature; it is a tragedy of the soul. When indifference replaces human empathy, society has lost its moral compass. It is a black mark on our collective humanity."

For human rights advocates, however, the public’s chilling reaction on Torregaveta beach did not occur in a vacuum. It comes amid an increasingly hostile political climate targeted directly at Italy's estimated 150,000 Roma people.

Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi’s right-wing coalition government recently declared a national "state of emergency" regarding the Roma population, officially framing the minority group as a threat to public security. Under the leadership of hardline Interior Minister Roberto Maroni, a member of the anti-immigrant Northern League party, the government initiated a controversial policy to census and fingerprint all Roma living in informal camps—including young children.

The fingerprinting scheme drew sharp rebuke from the European Parliament, the United Nations, and Amnesty International, who labeled the policy discriminatory and reminiscent of Fascist-era laws. Furthermore, recent months have seen a surge in anti-Roma violence, including vigilante arson attacks on Roma camps in Naples that forced hundreds of residents to flee under police escort.

Critics argue that the demonization of Roma migrants by political leaders has effectively dehumanized the community in the eyes of the Italian public.

"When the state treats an entire ethnic group as a security hazard rather than human beings, it sends a clear message to the population," said Juan de Dios Ramírez-Heredia, president of Union Romani. "The people on that beach didn't see two drowned little girls. They saw two 'gypsies' whose lives were worth less than their afternoon in the sun."

As the bodies of Cristina and Violetta were finally carried away in wooden coffins, the beachgoers slowly packed up their umbrellas and headed home. But while the tide will wash away the footprints on Torregaveta beach, the images of that afternoon have left a lasting mark on Italy—a nation now forced to look in the mirror and ask how its sunlit shores became a scene of such dark indifference.
